newsitem.title: USA: Two big U.S. insurers post solid first-quarter results.
newsitem.headline: Two big U.S. insurers post solid first-quarter results.

text.p: Two big U.S. insurers posted strong first-quarter earnings Thursday, helped by lower losses for catastrophes and good underwriting.
The Hartford insurance company saw its operating profits more than double in the first quarter as mild winter weather helped hold losses down.
American International Group Inc.'s operating profits rose about 16 percent on strong underwriting and good growth, especially in its domestic property-casualty business.
Earnings from both companies were in line to slightly better than analysts' First Call consensus estimates.

The Hartford's operating profits rose to $179 million, or $1.52 a share, compared with $84 million, or 72 cents a share, a year ago, topping Wall Street's First Call consensus estimate of $1.49 a share.

American International's operating income was $750.6 million, or $1.60 a share, compared with $652.3 million, or $1.38 a share in the year-ago quarter. The First Call consensus prediction was $1.58 a share.
The milder weather in the Northeast this winter was one factor behind The Hartford's improved profits and most likely helped American International as well, analysts said.

"The big gain year over year was really in the property-casualty business," Lehman analyst Peter Wade said of The Hartford. "Last year, you had a very diffficult quarter from a catastrophe loss perspective."
The Hartford, Conn.-based company said catastrophe losses from its North American property-casualty business were $16 million after tax compared with $77 million a year ago.
In addition, the drag on this quarter's profits was reduced after The Hartford's decision in October to boost reserves for asbestos and environmental losses, he said.
The Hartford also showed strength in its domestic property-casualty underwriting performance, Wade said.
The Hartford's North American net income, excluding catastrophes, rose 17 percent to $120 million and revenues rose 3 percent to $1.605 billion.
International operations, however, were a disappointment, with net income down 33 percent to $14 million despite an 8 percent rise in revenues.
The Hartford Chairman Ramani Ayer said the decline internationally was due primarily to difficult automobile market conditions in Britain.
Meanwhile, American International managed to post strong domestic growth despite tough U.S. market conditions.
In its general insurance business, domestic net premiums written, excluding the risk management business, gained 12.3 percent in the first quarter.
Overall general insurance net premiums written rose 6 percent after the impact of foreign exchange.
The life insurance business also showed unexpected strength, Salomon analyst Michael Smith said.
AIG's worldwide life insurance operations reported first-quarter 1997 pretax income before realised capital gains of $346 million, up 22.3 percent.
"Everything seems to be clicking on all cylinders and there were no great surprises," Nutmeg Securities analyst Ira Zuckerman said of AIG.
However, the recent strength of the dollar had an impact on the translation of foreign currency premiums into U.S. dollars.
In the foreign general insurance business, for instance, premium growth in the original currency was 8 percent, but dropped to 1.7 percent after the impact of foreign exchange.
